description:
Continuing the previous teenage study, Wesam Saad develops the movement from childhood control towards reasoning and personal responsibility. His central illustration distinguishes a protective fence from the work of drawing a young person towards Christ at the centre. Parents should retain boundaries against serious danger while using patient explanation and gospel conversation within them. He warns both against restrictions that leave no room to grow and against abandoning the responsibility to protect.

The discussion then considers strength, work and money. Saad presents physical strength as something to use for service, provision and protection rather than self-display. Earning money does not automatically overcome selfishness: a young person may simply replace parental funding with earnings spent entirely on personal wants. He therefore calls for deliberate instruction about generosity, household service and the use of resources for God’s glory.

The same purpose extends to rest and relationships. Saad encourages recreation that renews strength, exercises the mind or deepens relationships, while qualifying that he is not declaring all passive entertainment sinful. He also urges parents to help teenagers form relationships with mature Christians across age groups. Teaching about girls and sibling relationships is promised for a later session, leaving those parts of the course open.

questions.question: What is the intended movement from imposed correction to self-discipline?
questions.answer: Saad wants a young person increasingly to recognise temptation, understand the gospel reasons for holiness and participate in choosing appropriate restraint. The phone illustration models extended conversation rather than only immediate confiscation. This does not remove the parent’s limits: he explains that the same situation may require the parent to act if the young person refuses to recognise the danger.

questions.question: What is the difference between the fence and Christ at the centre of the illustration?
questions.answer: The fence represents protective boundaries against significant danger. Movement towards Christ represents growth in wisdom, holiness and understanding. Saad distinguishes enforcing the boundary from the patient reasoning and gracious conversation used to invite a young person towards Christ. He does not treat those two responsibilities as interchangeable.

questions.question: What two extremes does Saad warn parents to avoid?
questions.answer: One extreme replaces a fence with restrictions so tight that a teenager has no room to grow. The other supplies no meaningful boundaries because the parent avoids the difficulty of involvement. Saad argues for both protection and increasing freedom, with reasoning and patience within an affectionate relationship rather than either total control or indifference.

questions.question: How does the session interpret a young man’s developing strength?
questions.answer: Saad presents strength as a gift to be used in serving, providing for and protecting others. He contrasts that purpose with intimidation, fighting or self-display. The parent’s task in his account is to connect the young man’s developing abilities with responsibility for other people, not simply admiration of his own power.

questions.question: Why does earning money not automatically make a teenager responsible?
questions.answer: A child who once relied on parents for personal wants can earn wages and remain just as self-centred. Saad distinguishes funding oneself from accepting responsibility for others. His concern is that employment without instruction may merely supply a larger budget for the same selfish purposes, instead of preparing the young person for faithful adult life.

questions.question: What kind of preparation for earning and using money is proposed?
questions.answer: Saad recommends conversation and study about money before employment becomes an unchecked pattern. He illustrates planning generosity towards the church, members in need and the family, rather than treating every wage as personal spending money. Employment is described as a training ground in which parents continue to guide choices and the young person learns to use resources for God’s glory.

questions.question: How are service at home and rest connected with the wider aim?
questions.answer: Service is to take priority over entertainment when household work remains. Saad then extends the aim of glorifying God to rest itself. He commends activities that renew physical strength, stimulate thought or deepen a relationship, and explicitly says that he is not declaring every film or period of passive relaxation sinful.

questions.question: What challenge does Saad attach to the complaint of boredom?
questions.answer: He asks whether unused energy, ability and opportunity could be directed towards serving God or others instead of being kept entirely for personal comfort. Activities such as reading, exercise and time with family illustrate alternatives. His pastoral argument connects meaningful use of time with the larger purpose of training for responsibility, including the example of Paul praying while imprisoned.

questions.question: Why are relationships with older Christians encouraged?
questions.answer: Saad wants the desire for friendship to draw teenagers into the life of the church, where mature believers can contribute wisdom and experience. He explicitly says that friendships with other teenagers need not be stopped. The father remains responsible for discipling his son while welcoming the contribution of different godly men, rather than making age similarity the only basis for fellowship.
